Q1.answer: (a) Proclamation 11046, FR Doc. 2026-14991, 91 FR 46639: signed July 20, published July 23, 2026; imposes 50% section 338 duty on listed Canadian alcoholic beverages. It printed August 19, but the operative start was changed to 12:01 a.m. ET August 22, for goods entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption. (b) Proclamation 11047, FR Doc. 2026-14992, 91 FR 46653: signed July 20, published July 23; imposes the 50% duty on listed Canadian dairy products; same changed operative start and entry/withdrawal event. (c) Proclamation 11048, FR Doc. 2026-14997, 91 FR 46663: signed July 20, published July 23; imposes the 50% duty on listed Canadian motor-vehicle products; same changed operative start and entry/withdrawal event. (d) Proclamation 11056, FR Doc. 2026-17294, 91 FR 54789: signed August 18, published August 24; suspends the three duties for three days, sets their effective date to August 22 at 12:01 a.m. ET, and changes the Annex II chapeaux. Its date is measured against entry for consumption or withdrawal from warehouse for consumption. (e) Proclamation 11061, FR Doc. 2026-18835, 91 FR 58311: signed September 8, published September 14; excludes the alcoholic beverages in its Annex from importation starting September 29 at 12:01 a.m. ET, measured against importation. (f) Proclamation 11062, FR Doc. 2026-18836, 91 FR 58319: signed September 8, published September 14; same importation-based exclusion date for listed dairy products. (g) Proclamation 11063, FR Doc. 2026-18837, 91 FR 58325: signed September 8, published September 14; same importation-based exclusion date for listed motor-vehicle products. (h) Proclamation 11064, FR Doc. 2026-18838, 91 FR 58331: signed September 8, published September 14; effective September 15 at 12:01 a.m. ET for entries/withdrawals for consumption, it makes the products in its Annex I, Part A subject to the alcoholic-beverage duty and removes the Part B products from that duty. (i) Proclamation 11065, FR Doc. 2026-18839, 91 FR 58339: signed September 8, published September 14; effective September 15 at 12:01 a.m. ET for entries/withdrawals for consumption, it adds the motor-vehicle Part A products to the duty and removes the Part B products. It also says the modified duties apply in addition to section 232 duties. (j) Proclamation 11076, FR Doc. 2026-22292, 91 FR 68861: signed October 23, filed October 29, published October 30; effective October 30 at 12:01 a.m. ET for entries/withdrawals for consumption, it removes the motor-vehicle Part A products from the duty and adds the Part B products. The three exclusion proclamations use importation, not entry for consumption, as the trigger; the other effective changes described above use entry or withdrawal for consumption.
Q1.basis: The initial duty clauses are Proclamation 11046 cl. (1), 91 FR 46641; 11047 cl. (1), 91 FR 46654; and 11048 cl. (1), 91 FR 46665. Proclamation 11056 cl. (1), 91 FR 54790, changes the effective date to August 22 and amends the Annex II chapeaux. The exclusions are 11061 cl. (1), 91 FR 58312; 11062 cl. (1), 91 FR 58320; and 11063 cl. (1), 91 FR 58326. The scope changes are 11064 cl. (1), 91 FR 58332; 11065 cl. (1), 91 FR 58340; and 11076 cl. (1), 91 FR 68862. The documents’ publication/signing dates and first-page citations appear in their respective FR entries identified above.
Q1.uncertainty: The product lists and tariff headings in the Annexes are images, so I cannot enumerate the individual products/headings. The product-group effects above describe the readable operative text and the Annex Parts by which each document changes scope.

Q2.answer: (a) Entry 1, August 20 at 2:00 p.m.: $40,000 × 0% = $0 section 338 duty. Entry 2, August 21 at 11:59 p.m.: $40,000 × 0% = $0. Entry 3, August 22 at 12:01 a.m.: $40,000 × 50% = $20,000. The entry date/time controls, not the date the wine arrived. (b) Proclamation 11046 cl. (1) and its HTSUS-modification clause cl. (3) print August 19. Proclamation 11056 cl. (1) later sets the effective date to August 22 and expressly amends the chapeau of Annex II by deleting August 19 and inserting August 22. It does not amend the numbered clauses (1) or (3) of 11046, which therefore still print August 19. The later operative date in 11056, plus its Annex II amendment, controls; subsequent September proclamations also say the suspension lapsed and duties became effective August 22. (c) Proclamation 11056 says refunds required to implement it are processed under applicable law and CBP’s standard procedures. Since entry 1 predates the controlling start, the documents support a refund of a deposit for that entry, but do not promise an automatic refund or prescribe a procedure beyond applicable law and CBP’s standard procedures. (d) No further presidential action was required on August 22: 11056 itself set that date and the three-day suspension. Later proclamations state in their recitals that Canada reneged on August 21, ceased negotiating in good faith, and did not remove the discrimination; they say the suspension lapsed and duties became effective at 12:01 a.m. August 22. (e) The 30-day calculation printed in 11046 is July 20 signing/finding date plus 30 days: July 21–31 = 11 days; August 1–19 = 19 days; 11 + 19 = 30. That yielded the original August 19 start, later delayed three days to August 22.
Q2.basis: The original 50% rate and entry/withdrawal trigger are 11046 cl. (1), 91 FR 46641; the original date and 30-day rule are 11046 paras. 9–10, 91 FR 46640. The amendment is 11056 cl. (1), 91 FR 54790; refunds are cl. (4), 91 FR 54791. The account of Canada’s August 21 conduct and the August 22 lapse appears in the recitals of 11064 paras. 3–4, 91 FR 58331–32, and is repeated in 11061 para. 4, 91 FR 58312, and 11065 para. 4, 91 FR 58340.
Q2.uncertainty: The August 19 date remains in the unamended numbered clauses of 11046. The later proclamation and amended Annex II supply the controlling August 22 date, but the documents do not redraft those earlier clauses.

Q3.answer: (a) A: May be imported September 10; the September 29 exclusion has not begun. Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = $15,000. B: May be imported September 27 and placed in the warehouse. The goods were imported before September 29 but not entered for consumption until October 5, so they remain subject to the 50% duty: $30,000 × 50% = $15,000. C: May be imported at 11:30 p.m. September 28; its September 29 entry does not change that importation date. Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = $15,000. D: The September 29, 12:30 a.m. importation falls within the Annex exclusion; it may not be imported, so no lawful consumption entry or tariff total is available. (b) E was imported/admitted to the FTZ September 25, before the import exclusion begins. On October 6 it remains subject to the 50% duty on withdrawal for consumption: $30,000 × 50% = $15,000. It must be admitted in privileged foreign status unless eligible for domestic status. (c) If the exclusion is invalidated as applied to this beer, the 50% duty imposed by Proclamation 11046 applies to imports to which the invalidated ban had applied, under the exclusion proclamation’s severability clause. (d) No. The exclusion applies to products in its own Annex; it does not change the duty on listed Canadian alcoholic products outside that Annex.
Q3.basis: The alcoholic duty is 50% on Annex II products entered or withdrawn for consumption on or after August 22: 11046 cls. (1), (4), 91 FR 46641–42, as amended by 11056 cl. (1), 91 FR 54790. Proclamation 11061 cl. (1) makes the Annex exclusion effective for goods imported on or after September 29; cl. (2) keeps the 50% duty on covered goods imported earlier but not yet entered/withdrawn for consumption; cl. (3) preserves other duty scope; and cl. (9)(b) provides the invalidation fallback, 91 FR 58312–13. FTZ status is addressed in 11046 cl. (4), 91 FR 46641.
Q3.uncertainty: The text does not specify tariff treatment for an attempted unlawful import after the exclusion takes effect. The answers treat D as a prohibited import, not as a lawful import carrying a substitute tariff.

Q4.answer: (a) September 10 entries: X—section 232: $100,000 × 25% = $25,000; section 338: $0. Y—section 232: $100,000 × 25% = $25,000; section 338: $0. Z—section 232: $100,000 × 25% = $25,000; section 338: $0. The original alcoholic, dairy, and motor-vehicle proclamations all exclude articles subject to section 232 duties, and the September 15 scope amendments are not yet effective. (b) October 1 entries: X—section 232: $25,000; section 338: $0, because the alcoholic scope amendment does not say the alcoholic duty stacks with section 232 and the original section 232 exclusion remains. Y—section 232: $25,000; section 338: $0, because the dairy proclamation retains its section 232 exclusion. Z—section 232: $25,000; section 338: $100,000 × 50% = $50,000. The motor-vehicle scope proclamation says the modified motor-vehicle duty applies in addition to section 232 duties; Z remains on the original Annex II list and is not said to be removed by a scope list. (c) The assumed section 232 calculation is $100,000 × 25% = $25,000 for each product at both dates.
Q4.basis: The section 232 exceptions are 11046 cl. (2), 91 FR 46641; 11047 cl. (2), 91 FR 46655; and 11048 cl. (2), 91 FR 46665. The September alcoholic scope change is 11064 cl. (1), 91 FR 58332; unlike 11065, it does not state that the modified duty applies in addition to section 232. The motor-vehicle addition is expressly in 11065 cl. (1), 91 FR 58340, effective September 15. The duty rate and customs value for section 232 are the scenario assumptions.
Q4.uncertainty: The Annex Parts are images. The scenario expressly places these products on no other image list; the motor-vehicle conclusion reads the express stacking sentence in 11065 together with the unrepealed original Annex II coverage.

Q5.answer: (a) 3:00 p.m. September 14: P no; Q yes; R yes; S no. The September change is not yet effective, so only products on the original duty Annex II are covered. 12:01 a.m. September 15: P yes (September Part A adds it); Q no (September Part B removes it); R yes (original Annex II and September Part A); S no (not yet added by the October change). 4:00 p.m. October 29: P yes; Q no; R yes; S no. 12:01 a.m. October 30: P yes; Q no; R no (October Part A removes it); S yes (October Part B adds it). November 3: P yes; Q no; R no; S yes. Every yes is the 50% duty; every no is no section 338 duty. (b) Proclamation 11076 was signed October 23, filed with the Office of the Federal Register October 29 at 11:15 a.m., and published October 30. Its changes apply from 12:01 a.m. ET October 30 to goods entered for consumption or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption. It does not reach earlier entries and contains no refund provision. (c) P became dutiable seven days after the September 8 scope proclamation was signed; S became dutiable seven days after the October 23 scope proclamation was signed. The original finding proclamation was signed July 20: September 15 is 57 days later and October 30 is 102 days later. The scope proclamations recite section 338’s 30-day waiting period but do not explain whether that period runs from the original July 20 finding or restarts for the later scope changes.
Q5.basis: The September motor-vehicle scope change makes Part A subject and Part B no longer subject from September 15, 11065 cl. (1), 91 FR 58340. The October change reverses the treatment of its Parts A and B from October 30, 11076 cl. (1), 91 FR 68862. Its signature date is on the document’s first page, 91 FR 68861; filing is shown at 91 FR 68871. The original 50% duty and Annex II coverage are 11048 cl. (1), 91 FR 46665; its 30-day recital is para. 9, 91 FR 46664–65. The later scope proclamations’ 30-day recitals are 11065 para. 8, 91 FR 58340, and 11076 para. 9, 91 FR 68862.
Q5.uncertainty: The proclamations do not expressly address refunds for entries before the effective date, and provide no retroactive application in the operative scope clauses. The waiting-period text leaves open whether an amendment that adds products is measured from the original finding or the later scope proclamation’s finding.

Q6.answer: (a) On $100,000 with 4% MFN ($4,000): (1) Switzerland: section 301 8.5% × $100,000 = $8,500; MFN + section 301 = $12,500. (2) Norway: section 301 12.5% = $12,500; total = $16,500. (3) United Kingdom: section 301 10% = $10,000; total = $14,000. (4) Germany, as an EU product: target combined MFN plus section 301 is 10%; section 301 is 6% = $6,000; total = $10,000. (5) Taiwan: same 10% combined target; section 301 6% = $6,000; total = $10,000. (6) Türkiye: section 301 12.5% = $12,500; total = $16,500. (7) Japan: target combined rate 12.5%; section 301 8.5% = $8,500; total = $12,500. (8) Liechtenstein: $0 section 301 under this action; total MFN plus section 301 = $4,000. (9) Hong Kong: section 301 12.5% = $12,500; total = $16,500. (10) India: section 301 10% = $10,000; total = $14,000. (b) Section 301 only: Germany with 12% MFN, 0% × $100,000 = $0; Japan with 12% MFN, (12.5% − 12%) × $100,000 = $500; Taiwan with exactly 10% MFN, $0; South Korea with exactly 10% MFN, (12.5% − 10%) × $100,000 = $2,500; Switzerland duty-free MFN, 12.5% × $100,000 = $12,500. (c) Treatment differs from the June proposal for Germany/EU, Taiwan, Japan, and Switzerland: their stated target rate remained 10% (EU/Taiwan) or 12.5% (Japan/Switzerland), but the adopted action makes the section 301 rate net of MFN rather than a flat 10% or 12.5%. The stated rationale is consistency with reciprocal-trade arrangements and encouraging commitments. India changed from proposed 12.5% to adopted 10%; the final notice says India imposed a forced-labor import prohibition after the proposal. Norway, the UK, Türkiye, and Hong Kong retain the proposed direct 12.5%, 10%, 12.5%, and 12.5% treatment, respectively. Liechtenstein is not one of the 60 investigated economies and is not listed in the proposal or adopted rate lists.
Q6.basis: Adopted rates and net-MFN rules: USTR Notice, FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47320–21; specific country determinations include Japan at 91 FR 47324, Switzerland at 91 FR 47327, Taiwan at 91 FR 47327, and the general 12.5% rule at 91 FR 47321. The net-MFN method and threshold rules are also in the presidential memorandum section 1(a)(ii), FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47720. The June proposal’s 10% and 12.5% groups are in FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34274. The post-proposal bans/commitment and rationale are in FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47319 and 47320–21.
Q6.uncertainty: The forced-labor notice does not mention Liechtenstein or say that Liechtenstein is treated as Switzerland for origin purposes. The $0 answer is the reading of the enumerated 60-economy scope; any external origin rule equating the two is not established by these documents.

Q7.answer: (a) France is an EU member state. MFN equivalent = ($0.03/kg × 2,000 kg) ÷ $12,000 = $60 ÷ $12,000 = 0.5%. Section 301 rate = 10% − 0.5% = 9.5%; duty = $12,000 × 9.5% = $1,140. (b) Compound MFN duty = 4% × $20,000 ($800) + $0.25/kg × 4,000 kg ($1,000) = $1,800; equivalent = $1,800 ÷ $20,000 = 9%. Italy/EU: 10% − 9% = 1%; section 301 = $20,000 × 1% = $200. Japan: 12.5% − 9% = 3.5%; section 301 = $700. Brazil: direct 12.5%; section 301 = $20,000 × 12.5% = $2,500. (c) Column 1 equivalent = $2,200 ÷ $20,000 = 11%. Taiwan: MFN is above its 10% cap, so section 301 = $0. Switzerland: 12.5% − 11% = 1.5%; section 301 = $20,000 × 1.5% = $300. (d) The ad valorem-equivalent calculation for specific or compound column 1 rates is in U.S. note 52(k). The zero-duty result at or above the cap is in the memorandum’s operative section 1(a)(ii) and the adopted Notice’s corresponding rate determinations.
Q7.basis: The equivalent-rate rule, including its example, is U.S. note 52(k), FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47394. The 10% EU/Taiwan cap and 12.5% Japan/Korea/Switzerland cap, including zero section 301 duty at or above the cap, are in memorandum section 1(a)(ii), FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47720, and adopted Notice, FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47320–21. Brazil is in the direct 12.5% group, 91 FR 47321–22. Scenario rates, weights, values, and column 1 duty amounts are supplied in the question.

Q8.answer: (a) Dominican Republic is in the 12.5% direct-rate group; on each dutiable $80,000 shipment, section 301 = $80,000 × 12.5% = $10,000. 1. July 29 entry: $10,000; it was loaded before July 24 but entered after the July 28 exception deadline. 2. July 27 at 3:00 p.m.: $0; vessel-loaded and in transit before July 24, and entered before July 28 at 12:01 a.m. 3. July 28 at 12:01 a.m.: $10,000; the exception requires entry before that exact time. 4. July 27 entry: $10,000; it was loaded after the July 24 start, so it fails the transit exception. 5. July 23 entry: $0; before the general effective time. 6. July 26 warehouse withdrawal: $10,000; arrival in June is not the defined transit exception and withdrawal is after the effective time. 7. Air freight entered July 25: $10,000; the exception is limited to goods loaded onto a vessel, not an aircraft. (b) The goods-in-transit rule is in the DATES line of the adopted USTR Notice. (c) The President signed the memorandum July 23; the duties apply from 12:01 a.m. ET July 24; the action notice was published July 28. (d) July 30: the pharmaceutical exception is not effective yet, so $80,000 × 12.5% = $10,000. August 3: $0 section 301 duty, because the patented pharmaceutical article in heading 9903.04.62 is within the exemption effective July 31.
Q8.basis: The effective date and exact vessel-transit cutoff are the DATES line of USTR Notice, FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47318. Dominican Republic is not in the 10% or net-MFN groups, so the direct 12.5% rule applies, 91 FR 47320–21. The memorandum is FR Doc. 2026-15274, signed July 23 and published July 28, 91 FR 47717; the adopted Notice publication date is 91 FR 47318. The patented-pharmaceutical exception is U.S. note 52(f)(8), effective for entries/withdrawals on or after July 31, 91 FR 47394.

Q9.answer: (a) Thailand is in the direct 12.5% group. Under heading 9802.00.80, the dutiable value is $100,000 − $35,000 U.S. components = $65,000. Section 301 = $65,000 × 12.5% = $8,125. (b) Israel is in the direct 12.5% group. Under 9802.00.50, duty applies only to the $6,000 repair value: $6,000 × 12.5% = $750. (c) Mexico: (i) $0 section 301 when entered free of duty under USMCA; (ii) without the claim, $50,000 × 10% = $5,000. (d) $0: the Japanese passenger car is in heading 9903.94.01, expressly covered by the passenger-vehicle section 232 exemption in U.S. note 52(f)(2). (e) Brazil: $100,000 × 12.5% = $12,500. The fact that a good bears a section 232 duty does not itself exempt it; the named section 232 categories in U.S. note 52(f) do not include the assumed heading. (f) The June proposal said its exemptions included informational materials, donations, accompanied baggage, and all articles and parts subject to section 232. The adopted readable text has no general informational-materials or donations exemption; its baggage exception is for personal-use products in accompanied baggage. It exempts only the section 232 product categories specifically listed in U.S. note 52(f), not every item bearing a section 232 duty. Particular products may also be covered by Annex image lists, which cannot be read here.
Q9.basis: The 9802 valuation rules and the personal-use baggage exception are in U.S. note 52(a), FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47352. The proposed general exemptions are in FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34274 and 34276. The adopted section 232 exemptions are in U.S. note 52(f), 91 FR 47362–63; the specific vehicle exception is subdivision (f)(2), 91 FR 47362. Mexico’s USMCA exception is U.S. note 52(h), 91 FR 47363. The rate groups are in the adopted Notice, 91 FR 47320–21.
Q9.uncertainty: The Annex product lists are images. The answer to (f) concerns the readable operative text; the documents could provide product-specific exemptions in the image annexes.

Q10.answer: (a) September 10, 2026: MFN $200,000 × 3% = $6,000; section 232 $200,000 × 50% = $100,000; section 338 $0; section 301 $0; total duties listed = $106,000. The original motor-vehicle proclamation excludes section 232 articles, and the September scope change has not yet taken effect. (b) September 16: MFN $6,000; section 232 $100,000; section 338 $200,000 × 50% = $100,000; section 301 $0; total = $206,000. From September 15 the motor-vehicle proclamation’s modified duties apply in addition to section 232; this product remains on the original Annex II list and is not removed by a Part B or exclusion list. The section 301 duty is zero on both dates because the product is an aluminum article provided for under section 232 heading 9903.82.02, a listed section 301 exception. (c) September 1 with USMCA claim: section 338 $60,000 × 50% = $30,000; section 301 $0; total = $30,000. The USMCA claim exempts the Canadian product from the forced-labor section 301 duty, not from section 338. (d) September 1 without USMCA claim: section 338 $30,000; section 301 $60,000 × 10% = $6,000; total = $36,000. (e) A shipment imported October 2 that is in the alcoholic-beverage exclusion Annex is prohibited from importation from September 29. There is no lawful import-duty total for it. If one assumes a consumption entry is nevertheless filed, with no USMCA claim, the section 301 calculation would be $60,000 × 10% = $6,000; the exclusion proclamation does not state a substitute section 338 tariff for an unlawful post-ban import. (f) No. The IEEPA northern-border duties were ordered to be ended by Executive Order 14389; the temporary 10% surcharge was limited through July 24, 2026. Neither is in force for September entries. In any event, the surcharge expressly does not apply in addition to section 232 duties.
Q10.basis: For (a)–(b), the original section 232 exception is Proclamation 11048 cl. (2), 91 FR 46665; the later stacking rule and September 15 effective date are Proclamation 11065 cl. (1), 91 FR 58340. The forced-labor section 232 exception is U.S. note 52(f)(1), FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47362; Canada’s USMCA exception is note 52(g), 91 FR 47363; Canada’s direct rate is 10%, 91 FR 47320. The alcoholic import ban is Proclamation 11061 cl. (1), 91 FR 58312. IEEPA termination is Executive Order 14389 secs. 1–2, FR Doc. 2026-03832, 91 FR 9437–38. The surcharge’s term is Proclamation 11012 cl. (7), and its section 232 rule is cl. (4), FR Doc. 2026-03824, 91 FR 9342–43.
Q10.uncertainty: For (e), the text clearly prohibits the importation but does not specify a tariff fallback for an unlawful post-ban import. The hypothetical section 301 calculation is not permission to import.

Q11.answer: (a) Section 338 date mismatch: the July proclamations’ operative clauses still say August 19 (11046 cl. (1), 91 FR 46641; 11047 cl. (1), 91 FR 46654; 11048 cl. (1), 91 FR 46665). Proclamation 11056 cl. (1), 91 FR 54790, instead sets the effective date at August 22 and says it amends the Annex II chapeau by replacing August 19 with August 22; it does not amend the original numbered clauses (1) and (3). Thus the amended Annex and later effective-date instruction say August 22 while the old numbered clauses still print August 19. The September recitals repeat the obsolete August 19 effective-date description and then say the suspension lapsed and duties became effective August 22: 11061 paras. 1 and 4, 91 FR 58311–12; 11062 paras. 1 and 4, 91 FR 58319–20; 11063 paras. 1 and 4, 91 FR 58325–26; 11064 paras. 1–4, 91 FR 58331–32; 11065 paras. 1–4, 91 FR 58339–40; and 11076 paras. 1–4, 91 FR 68861–62. These are the same date discrepancy repeated, not separate substantive changes. (b) There is a facial 30-day timing tension in the scope proclamations: they recite that section 338 duties may not take effect earlier than 30 days after a presidential finding, while the September 8 and October 23 scope proclamations apply changes seven days after signing (11065 cl. (1), 91 FR 58340; 11076 cl. (1), 91 FR 68862). The original July 20 finding had already preceded those dates by more than 30 days, but the documents do not explain whether the waiting period restarts for a later finding or product-scope addition. (c) In the forced-labor action, the June proposal described blanket exemptions for all section 232 articles and parts, informational materials, donations, and accompanied baggage (FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34274, 34276). The adopted readable tariff note instead expressly limits baggage to personal-use products and lists particular section 232 categories; it does not provide a blanket informational-materials, donations, or all-section-232 exemption (U.S. note 52(a), (f), FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47352, 47362–63). A section 232 article under a heading not named in note 52(f) remains subject to section 301, as illustrated by note 52(a)’s general rule and the assumed case in Q9(e). This is a proposal/adoption difference, not by itself a discrepancy. The potential discrepancy is the July Notice’s statement that USTR exempted all products proposed in Annex A except non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemicals (91 FR 47330), insofar as that is read to describe the general exemptions too; the operative note does not preserve those general categories. The Notice’s Annex-A-specific wording may be narrower than such a reading.
Q11.basis: The cited operative and recital passages distinguish effective-date provisions from preamble recitals. The forced-labor proposal’s exemption description is FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34274–76; adopted note 52 is FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47352 and 47362–63; the adopted Notice’s Annex-A statement is 91 FR 47330.
Q11.uncertainty: The forced-labor Annexes are partly images. The apparent mismatch between the July Notice’s statement about retaining Annex A products and the adopted general exemption categories depends on whether that statement is read to cover exemptions outside Annex A. The 30-day waiting-period issue is a facial tension, not a resolved legal conclusion, because the documents do not specify which finding controls for amendments.

Q12.answer: (a) Cambodia, aloe etc.: specifically exempt, $0. Malaysia: no readable product-specific exemption for this item; $60,000 × 10% = $6,000. (b) Malaysia Boswellia: specifically exempt, $0. Taiwan Boswellia: specifically exempt, $0. Bangladesh: no readable Boswellia exemption; $100,000 × 10% = $10,000. Argentina: no readable Boswellia exemption; $100,000 × 10% = $10,000. (c) Taiwan argan oil: specifically exempt, $0. Japan: MFN 4% leaves 8.5% to its 12.5% cap; $100,000 × 8.5% = $8,500. Indonesia: direct 10%; $100,000 × 10% = $10,000. (d) Sesame seeds for sowing under 1207.40.00 are expressly exempt for all investigated economies: $0 for Japan, Mexico, and Thailand. (e) Cambodia psyllium: specifically exempt, $0. Thailand: direct 12.5%; $40,000 × 12.5% = $5,000. El Salvador: direct 10%; $40,000 × 10% = $4,000. Italy/EU: 10% combined cap less 2% MFN = 8%; $40,000 × 8% = $3,200.
Q12.basis: Country rates: FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47320–22, 47327. All-economy sesame sowing-seed exemption is U.S. note 52(c)(4), 91 FR 47356. Malaysia’s Boswellia/argan/psyllium exemptions are note 52(j)(4)(ii), 91 FR 47365; Cambodia’s Boswellia/aloe/psyllium exemptions are note 52(j)(5)(ii), 91 FR 47366; El Salvador’s aloe exemption is note 52(j)(7)(ii), 91 FR 47375; Argentina and Bangladesh exceptions are note 52(j)(8)–(9), 91 FR 47383; Taiwan’s listed product exceptions are note 52(j)(10), 91 FR 47383–84. The Taiwan, Japan, and EU net-MFN thresholds and the equivalent-rate rule are note 52(k), 91 FR 47394.
Q12.uncertainty: The Annex II product lists are images. These calculations assume no image-list exemption beyond the specific product/country exclusions readable in the text, as directed by the scenario assumptions.

Q13.answer: (a) U.S.-produced parts are $60,000; non-U.S. content is $200,000 − $60,000 = $140,000. Section 232 = $140,000 × 25% = $35,000. The 15% floor on the full $200,000 is $30,000, so $35,000 controls. (b) No U.S. parts: $200,000 × 25% = $50,000; this exceeds the $30,000 floor. (c) Not USMCA-qualifying: the special non-U.S.-content rule does not apply; $200,000 × 25% = $50,000. (d) Japan is in the 15% combined Column 1 plus section 232 group. MFN = $200,000 × 2.5% = $5,000; section 232 fills 15% − 2.5% = 12.5%; $200,000 × 12.5% = $25,000. (e) Only $20,000 is value attributable to U.S.-produced parts, so non-U.S. content is $180,000; $180,000 × 25% = $45,000. The additional $30,000 attributed to U.S.-smelted/cast aluminum in a part made in Canada is not a U.S.-produced part and is not deducted under clause (2)(d). The stipulated majority of metal by weight is non-U.S., so the entirely-U.S.-metal lower rate does not apply. The $45,000 exceeds the $30,000 floor. (f) Same as (e), even for the October 6 entry: $45,000. The applicable Annex I-C treatment was already effective June 8. (g) Non-U.S. content is $200,000 − $140,000 = $60,000; 25% = $15,000, but the 15% full-value floor is $30,000, so section 232 = $30,000. (h) The special treatment applies through 11:59 p.m. ET December 31, 2027. Beginning January 1, 2028, the rates specified in clause (3) of Proclamation 11021 apply to Annex I-C products; the temporary USMCA non-U.S.-content formula no longer governs.
Q13.basis: Proclamation 11032 cl. (2), 91 FR 34087–88, establishes the Annex I-C rates, the Japan/other listed-jurisdiction MFN net-15% rule, the Canadian/Mexican USMCA non-U.S.-content formula and 15% floor; cl. (3), 91 FR 34088, sets January 1, 2028 as the transition to Proclamation 11021 cl. (3). The 85%-by-weight threshold for entirely U.S.-metal content is 11032 cl. (4), 91 FR 34088. The April proclamation’s full-value section 232 regime and 50% Annex I-A rate are 11021 cls. (1)–(2), FR Doc. 2026-06960, 91 FR 18203–04. All given values, content amounts, MFN rate for Canada, and Annex membership are scenario assumptions.
Q13.uncertainty: Annex IV, which 11032 references for details of the floor, is an image and not readable here. The answer applies the readable clause’s stated deduction and 15% minimum. No other readable tariff change makes October 6 differ from October 20.

Q14.answer: 1. Partly correct: the memorandum’s preamble says USTR expected the TRQs to be feasible by September 1, 2026, but its operative section 2 says to establish them as soon as USTR determines they are feasible; it does not set a September 1 deadline. 2. Incorrect as stated: the more-than-450 comments and nearly-60-witness figures belong to the earlier March initiation process and April hearings, not comments on the June proposal. After the June proposal, the adopted Notice reports over 1,600 written comments and over 100 hearing witnesses. 3. Incorrect: four economies—Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, and Trinidad and Tobago—moved from 12.5% to 10% after imposing bans; Cambodia and Guatemala were already proposed at 10% based on ART commitments. Jordan also moved to 10%, but because of an ART commitment, not an import ban. 4. Incorrect: commenters opposed beef and avocado exemptions, including by linking beef to forced labor, but USTR expressly determined not to remove those products from the exemption list. 5. Incorrect: the net-MFN economies are the EU, Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and Switzerland; the Notice does not give each a negotiated product-exemption list. The listed agreement-related exemptions cover only specified economies, and the Annex II table of contents has no separate Japan or South Korea part. 6. Partly correct: USTR says it exempted 471 additional products, but the adopted text says certain sugar and sugar-containing products, not all such products. 7. Incorrect: the 12.5% combined cap applies only to Japan, Korea, and Switzerland; EU and Taiwan have a 10% cap. Other economies’ section 301 rates are additional to MFN, so total duties can exceed 12.5%. 8. Correct: products subject to the duty admitted to an FTZ after the duty starts generally must be privileged foreign status, except products eligible for domestic status. 9. Correct: the adopted Notice says if an exemption is invalidated, the applicable tariff applies to imports that exemption covered before invalidation. 10. Correct as to the proposed Annex A list: USTR retained its proposed exemptions except for limiting certain chemicals to pharmaceutical applications. Separately, it adopted 471 additional exemptions.
Q14.basis: The TRQ feasibility forecast and operative direction are in the presidential memorandum preamble and section 2, FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47720–21. Initial and post-proposal comment/hearing counts are FR Docs. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34273, and 2026-15181, 91 FR 47319. Rate changes and later bans/ART commitments are 2026-15181, 91 FR 47319–21. Beef/avocado discussion and decision are 91 FR 47331. Net-MFN treatment is 91 FR 47320–21 and Annex II contents 91 FR 47395. The 471 additional products and certain sugar products are 91 FR 47331. The FTZ rule is 91 FR 47321; invalid-exemption rule is 91 FR 47335. The proposed Annex A decision is 91 FR 47330.
Q14.uncertainty: The Annexes are images, so this answer cannot independently audit every listed product or negotiated exemption. The statement about the TRQ deadline is partly correct only because September 1 appears as a preamble forecast, not as an operative deadline.

Q15.answer: All amounts below are additional to MFN; each entry has a $100,000 value. Case N is not USMCA-qualifying; Case U is USMCA-qualifying and claimed. 1. February 10, 2025: N $0; U $0. The northern-border duty was paused until March 4; the aluminum section 232 change did not start until March 12. 2. March 6, 2025: N border IEEPA duty $100,000 × 25% = $25,000; U same $25,000, because the USMCA border-duty exemption did not begin until March 7. 3. March 10, 2025: N border IEEPA $25,000; U $0, because its USMCA claim is exempt from the border duty from March 7 and the aluminum section 232 duty has not started. 4. March 14, 2025: N border IEEPA $25,000; U section 232 $100,000 × 25% = $25,000. The non-stacking rule then gave the Canada border IEEPA duty priority over section 232 for N; U is exempt from the border duty and bears section 232. 5. June 3, 2025: N border IEEPA $25,000; U section 232 $25,000. June 4 is the change in both section 232 rate and stacking priority. 6. June 10, 2025: N and U each section 232 $100,000 × 50% = $50,000; the section 232 duty now takes priority over the Canada border IEEPA duty. 7. August 5, 2025: N and U each section 232 $50,000. The later 35% northern-border rate does not stack on this section 232 article. 8. March 2, 2026: N and U each section 232 $50,000. 9. June 10, 2026: N and U each section 232 $50,000. 10. July 27, 2026: N and U each section 232 $50,000. 11. August 25, 2026: N and U each section 232 $50,000. 12. September 14, 2026: N and U each section 232 $50,000. 13. September 16, 2026: N and U each section 232 $50,000 plus section 338 $100,000 × 50% = $50,000; total additional duties $100,000. 14. November 10, 2026: same—section 232 $50,000 plus section 338 $50,000; total $100,000. Section 301 is $0 in both cases from July 24 onward because the article is in heading 9903.82.02, a listed section 232 article exemption. For Case U, the separate Canada-USMCA section 301 exemption also applies. The 338 section 232 exclusion remains in force through September 14; the September 15 motor-vehicle scope proclamation then expressly makes the modified section 338 duty additive to section 232. The extrusion remains covered by the original motor-vehicle Annex II and is not on a removal list. Other Canada duties: the 10% temporary import surcharge is not owed on any date—it was not yet effective for the 2025 dates, and in 2026 this section 232 article is excluded; it ended July 24. The reciprocal IEEPA tariff is not owed on this aluminum article while section 232 applies because the reciprocal order excludes section 232 steel/aluminum articles and future section 232 articles. The forced-labor section 301 duty is not owed from July 24 onward because of the express section 232 article exemption. The northern-border IEEPA duty is not owed for Case U from March 7 because of USMCA; for Case N it is owed at 25% on the specified March–June 3 entries, but does not stack on the section 232 article from June 4 and was terminated in 2026. Section 338 is not owed before its August 22 start or from August 22 through September 14 because the original proclamation excludes section 232 goods; it is owed from September 15 under the motor-vehicle modification.

Q15.uncertainty: The assumed Annex membership and heading are supplied by the question. The Section 122 and reciprocal provisions reference image annexes, but the readable text independently exempts section 232 articles; no image-list exemption is needed for these goods.
